World.title: 'Like I'd been ripped off': Life after a Parkinson's diagnosis at 41
World.content:
Parkinson's disease has often been referred to as an 'old man's disease', but for one northern Tasmanian mum, this could not be further from the truth.

Hayley Milne was diagnosed with early onset Parkinson's disease 10 years ago, at just 41 years old.

"I was working, had three children who were seven, nine and 11," Ms Milne said.

" It was like it'd been ripped off — most people get it in their 60s, 70s, 80s and then I get it in my 40s, where you're still having to do everything, it's the busiest time of your life. "

Symptoms of the neurological condition began in her mid-30s and have grown progressively worse over time.

"I have tremors in my head and my hands, my legs freeze, my balance is terrible, I don't have much of a memory," she said.

Hayley Milne (second from left) with her three children. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The disease, which impacts up to 150,000 Australians, reshaped the future Ms Milne thought she would have.

"I always enjoyed working but I stopped doing that 10 years ago," she said.

"I don't drive anymore, I don't write anymore, burning myself, dropping stuff, spilling stuff.

"For quite a few years I was very isolated at home because the anxiety and depression was horrific that I didn't like leaving my safe place.

"It took a lot to get over that grieving time, to go, you know, life's changing, however, there's nothing we can do to change it [back], so we've just got to keep going."

The disease has impacted Hayley Milne's memory, balance and ability to complete simple tasks. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Cases growing in the state

Parkinson's disease is the fastest-growing neurological condition in the world and Tasmania has some of the highest rates in the country.

Launceston local Peter Longman downplayed his Parkinson's symptoms for close to a decade before being left with no option but to confront his diagnosis three years ago.

Mr Longman's symptoms impact nearly every aspect of his life.

"It's turned it [my life] completely upside down from the simplest thing that I used to do," he said.

Peter Longman used to be very active, but his Parkinson's diagnosis turned his life "upside down". (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Mr Longman had always been very active.

"I'd wake up in the morning, and I'd go for a jog up the street, whether it was rain, wind or shine," he said.

"But you wouldn't catch me doing it nowadays."

Now, getting out of a chair is hard for Mr Longman.

Daphne Longman said it was heartbreaking to see the disease "stealing" her husband.

"He was a very athletic man up until three, four years ago, he did the Cradle to Coast 75-kilometre bike ride, he bushwalked, he kayaked — he can't do any of that now," she said.

" To see him not be able to do all the things that he loves doing, that's very painful for me. "

Daphne Longman says it's "painful" to see how the disease is impacting the man she loves. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The disease also impacts Mr Longman mentally.

"He'll be trying to speak to somebody, and he loses the sentence in the middle," Ms Longman said.

" For a man who is very intelligent and very witty and very clever, that's very frustrating for him. "

Tasmania chosen for global study

Despite experts predicting the disease will double in the next 20 years, little is actually known about what causes it, who it can impact, and how to treat it.

An international study is hoping to expand worldwide genetic research into Parkinson's disease and Tasmania has been chosen to contribute.

Hopes new injection will be a 'game-changer' for Parkinson's Scientists from the University of South Australia say the injection is designed to replace the need for multiple daily oral medications.

The University of Tasmania has been funded by both the Shake It Up Foundation and Global Parkinson's Genetic Program to collect blood samples from Tasmanians living with and without Parkinson's disease.

UTAS researcher Samantha Bramich is one of those leading the initiative in Tasmania and is encouraging all Tasmanians to join the genetic study.

"We're really lucky to have been invited to contribute to this worldwide project, which is hopefully going to provide some important breakthroughs in our understanding of the genetics of Parkinson's," Dr Bramich said.

"We need better treatments and potentially disease-modifying treatments to prevent and cure it, but, in order to do that, we need to know more about the genetics behind Parkinson's."

Dr Samantha Bramich is hoping blood samples from Tasmanians will help researchers better understand what causes Parkinson's. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

For fellow Parkinson's researcher Michele Callisaya, this study hits close to home.

"I was diagnosed just over four years ago, but I had symptoms for probably two or three years before that," Dr Callisaya said.

" Hearing those words, 'You have Parkinson's', was very devastating and still a bit unbelievable. "

Like Ms Milne, Dr Callisaya received her diagnosis in her 40s.

"The diagnosis really brought me into trying to do more research to improve care," Dr Callisaya said.

Dr Callisaya has already rolled up her sleeve for the global study and hopes to see others do the same.

"Traditionally, we don't get things like the clinical trials and the big studies coming to Tasmania, so it's a fantastic opportunity," she said.

" The fact that Tasmanians can now have an opportunity to participate in research that actually might find something that could stop or at least slow the progression of Parkinson's is incredible. "

Michele Callisaya was diagnosed with Parkinson's when she was in her 40s. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

'Willing to do anything'

Ms Longman hopes the study will give her and her husband more answers.

"It's stealing his life," she said.

"To see Peter, who to me wasn't an old man, and who was so fit and active, to be becoming debilitated by this disease was frustrating and my nurse mind wanted to find out the causes.

"All these questions are on my mind and none of them have been answered."

Daphne and Peter Longman are "willing to participate in anything" which helps in the search for answers. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

She knows her husband may not receive any of the benefits but hopes it will help people diagnosed in the future.

"We're willing to participate in anything that helps," she said.

World.title: Trump concludes meeting on potential Iran deal without announcing decision
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has not announced a decision after concluding a two-hour meeting with his advisers on whether to move forward with a deal to extend the Iran ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran said the agreement had not been finalised. The Trump administration has not yet commented on the outcome of the White House Situation Room meeting.

Ahead of the meeting, Mr Trump said he was looking to make a "final determination" on a tentative deal. A senior administration official later said the meeting with national security aides had concluded.

The official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, would not say whether Mr Trump had made a decision to sign off on the tentative agreement.

The key sticking points holding up a US-Iran deal A possible US-Iran agreement is taking shape, but the toughest issues are still unsettled.

Mr Trump confirmed the high-level talks the day after the Associated Press and other news outlets reported that US and Iranian negotiators had come to terms on a tentative agreement.

The deal would extend the fragile ceasefire by 60 days as new talks are held on Iran's disputed nuclear program.

Mr Trump wrote on social media that "Iran must agree that they will never have a Nuclear Weapon or Bomb". He said the strait must be reopened for international navigation and all sea mines destroyed.

On Friday, Iran's main negotiator said he had "no trust in guarantees or words," only actions, underscoring lingering distrust after the US and Israel have twice attacked Iran over the past year while it was engaged in nuclear negotiations.

"No step will be taken before the other side acts," Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf wrote on X.

"We do not gain concessions through talks, but through missiles."

Nuclear issues remain unresolved

Later, but before Mr Trump's meeting concluded, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei told a state broadcaster that the agreement "has not been finalised yet".

On Thursday, US Vice-President JD Vance suggested negotiators were trying to strike general terms on Iran's nuclear program, with the specifics to be hammered out in the ensuing talks.

Mr Trump and his team said from the start of the conflict that a prime objective was to ensure that Iran could never have a nuclear weapon, but Mr Vance framed the war's accomplishments more modestly.

"We're in a position where we could substantially set back their nuclear program, not just during the term of this president but over the long term," Mr Vance said, adding that it would be "very, very good" for Americans.

Mr Baghaei, however, said on Friday that Iranian officials were "focused on the end of war and are not discussing the details of the nuclear plan at this point".

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei says an agreement has not been finalised yet. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Iran also wants any deal to include a truce between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah militants in Lebanon, where fighting has intensified despite a nominal ceasefire.

The Islamic Republic has 440.9 kilograms of uranium that is enriched up to 60 per cent purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90 per cent, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Iran has long maintained its nuclear program is peaceful and has not publicly committed to giving up the stockpile. It is believed to be buried under three nuclear sites that were badly damaged by US strikes last year.

Mr Trump returned on Friday to his on-and-off demand for the removal of the cache as part of a deal. The material would be unearthed by the US, in coordination with Iran and the IAEA, "and DESTROYED," he posted.

Deal would reopen the Strait of Hormuz

The proposed memorandum makes clear that Iran would not be able to impose tolls on the Strait of Hormuz and that it would have to remove all mines from the vital waterway within 30 days, according to a US official who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.

The US would gradually lift its blockade on Iranian ports and would also agree to relax sanctions, allowing Iran to sell more of its oil.

A vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, off the coast of Oman's Musandam province. (Reuters)

Mr Baghaei said Iran and Oman, which lie on opposite sides of the strait, would manage it and "adopt mechanisms" for transit through it, "based on their own national interests and the interests of the international community".

The two nations' foreign ministers discussed the issue by phone earlier on Friday, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who wrote on X that he had expressed solidarity "in the face of any threat".

On Wednesday, Mr Trump had warned Oman — a US ally — not to enter into any agreement with Iran to share control of the strait or the US will "have to blow them up".

Iran has effectively closed the strait since the US and Israel launched a surprise attack on February 28 that killed the Islamic Republic's supreme leader and other top officials.

Inside the Tehran press conference where the ABC was the only Western media present While on assignment inside Iran, our reporter asked a foreign ministry official about the regime's plan for the Strait of Hormuz.

Before then, the waterway was open to international traffic and around a fifth of the world's oil and gas passed through it.

The closure of the strait has caused the price of fuel and other goods to soar, with the effects felt far beyond the Middle East.

Iran has said it lets some commercial vessels pass — about two dozen daily in recent days, compared with more than 100 a day before the war.

But the Islamic Republic also has charged transit fees for at least some ships and established a formal gatekeeper agency earlier this month, spurring a new round of US sanctions this week.

Since the ceasefire began about seven weeks ago, the US and Iran have traded strikes and accusations of ceasefire violations.

But they have not returned to full-scale hostilities and have kept negotiating.

ABC/AP

World.title: Will Ruth Forrest get an apology for her leaked email?
World.content:
Ruth Forrest wants an apology. Will she get one?

The Member for Murchison, was livid on Tuesday night after an email she sent to the government was leaked to the media.

"I ask not only who, but why? What was the purpose — to embarrass me? To mock a legitimate health-related request? If so, that tells a great deal about the character of those involved," she said.

All she did, in that email, was ask for those appearing in front of her Estimates committee next week to refrain from wearing strong cologne or perfume.

"I and some others have experienced adverse reactions in the past to these strong fragrances, perfumes and aftershaves. I know I'm not alone in this," she wrote.

A simple request she says, and one that anyone who has been nasally attacked in an elevator can sympathise with.

Ms Forrest says the email contained private health information. (ABC News: Peter Curtis)

Nevertheless, someone in the executive building with a penchant for Santal 33 saw this as an affront to their rights, dropping it to local news outlet Pulse Tasmania.

"I call on the government, and I expect the leader will take this forward, to identify and name who was responsible, and to explain to this house, why a confidential internal email ended up in the hands of the media," Ms Forrest said.

You'd think the culprit would be easy to sniff out — follow the floral top notes.

'Deeply disappointed': Premier silent on leaked email complaint Ruth Forrest says she is "deeply disappointed" about a lack of government response over a leaked email and is now considering escalating her complaint.

Pulse Tasmania reported the Tasmanian legislative council member's (MLC's) request, and included her explanation for the request.

Was this a targeted smear from the government? Or just a disgruntled staffer who thought it was unreasonable?

Does it matter?

Ms Forrest wants an apology for the leaking of her email, which she says contained private health information.

What's been odd, is the complete reluctance from the government to offer one.

Deputy Premier Guy Barnett was asked on Thursday if the government was looking into it.

He couldn't comment — he said he hadn't seen the letter.

Guy Barnett said that if concerns had been raised, he was sure they would be "considered carefully". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Would the government apologise?

The deputy had no further comment.

Did he sympathise with Ruth Forrest?

He hadn't seen it.

After more questions, Mr Barnett offered that if concerns had been raised, he was sure they would be "considered carefully".

The next day, Health Minister Bridget Archer said she wasn't aware of it.

It's near impossible Ms Forrest's call for an apology has not made its way to the government.

The government does not want to apologise.

Relationship turns frosty

It's clear that the relationship between Ms Forrest and the government has deteriorated significantly.

On multiple occasions, she's been vocal about the Tasmanian government's "disrespect for the upper house", in ramming legislation through the chamber, or withdrawing it without notice.

The trigger point appears to have been last August, when she accepted an offer from Labor to take on the role of treasurer if the party was to claim government.

Could you blame her for saying yes?

It's clear that decision is viewed as a red stain on her independence.

The Tasmanian government's working attitude appears to have evaporated when it comes to the upper house. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

However, she remains an independent member of parliament, whose vote can help the government pass bills.

Ms Forrest's influence in the upper house cannot be understated.

Look to the chamber's seating plan — the newest member traditionally sits next to her to be shown the ropes.

Currently in that spot is Huon MLC Clare Glade-Wright, who this week condemned the leaking in a facebook post.

"Throwing mud at my colleagues is disappointing and goes against a safe and respectful workplace culture that I would expect from this place," she wrote.

Upper house a 'rubber stamp'?

To its credit, over the past three years the Rockliff government has gotten a lot better at governing in a hung parliament.

Three MPs share mental health struggles A national study has found 70 per cent of politicians feel their job is affecting their mental health. The ABC spoke to three Tasmanian MPs, including the state's premier, about their experiences.

In parliamentary debates, it's been willing to fall on its sword when a loss was certain.

It also made major, politically costly, concessions to win over progressive crossbenchers and stay in power.

Some include agreeing to review the salmon industry and to ban greyhound racing.

But that working attitude appears to have evaporated when it comes to the upper house.

Ruth Forrest is one of a small group of centrist independents who decide the fate of many pieces of legislation, most of whom the government seems determined to put offside.

Take the government's emergency fuel laws passed in March.

The Tasmanian Liberals announced a wind-down of the greyhound racing industry ahead of the last state election. (AAP: David Moir)

They were pushed through parliament late at night, having only been announced earlier that day.

MLC Mike Gaffney questioned if the chamber was becoming a "rubber stamp".

Casey Hiscutt said he was being asked to deal with legislation he had not formed an opinion on.

Last month, legislation to phase out greyhound racing was pulled at the last minute when the government realised its passage was not secured.

Bec Thomas said it showed "complete disrespect to the house and for us members".

MLC Mike Gaffney questioned if the chamber was becoming a "rubber stamp". (ABC News: Luke Bowden )

In the case of greyhounds, two votes are needed out of upper house members Rosemary Armitage, Mike Gaffney and Ruth Forrest for the bill to pass.

Has the government helped its case in the way it's treated that legislation, or those members?

It is the government's right to bring on its legislation as it pleases.

It could be fairly argued that all members of parliament should be more flexible.

But the ask of those MLCs seems fairly simple — work with us, and don't surprise us.

MLCs are are process-driven people, and they want to do their job properly.

Ignore that at your peril.

World.title: We asked for your modern dating love stories — here is what you told us
World.content:
Loading...

Technology promises better connections with people, but does it work when it comes to finding love?

We asked ABC readers to share their experiences with modern dating.

Here are your stories, from mustering the courage to speak to strangers, to striking out and striking gold on the dating apps.

Want to contribute your modern-dating experience? Share it here.

A little courage goes a long way

After months of matching with bots, women selling services or being left on "read", I gave multiple rounds of speed dating a crack.

When that failed as well, I started to question whether it was me or my background. I went into a dark place and my life started to spiral.

But the silver lining of failures in both forms was the courage I developed as an introvert.

After noticing a gorgeous woman on the train, I worked up the courage to speak to her. We met the following week for a coffee, which turned into dinner.

She pulled me out of a negative spiral. Ten years in, and happily married for six, I owe her my life and we both couldn't be happier.

To everyone: Dress well, be polite and respectful. It is possible to meet good people in real life.

— Aditya in NSW

Third time's the charm

Modern-day dating was terrifying, exciting and more often than not disappointing.

After a few months on Hinge and Bumble, I developed the all-too-famous cynicism that comes with strings of catfish attempts, dishonest intentions when meeting in real life and classic ghosting.

I was 31, tired and done. Resigned to a life of empowered spinsterhood.

I gave myself one more week. I went on three dates and finally, on that final date, there he was. Real, honest, hilarious, immensely kind and … did I say real?

What I did differently this time, however, was put all my needs and expectations on the table — then and there. No games, no wiggle room for future excuses.

Four years on — we are happily married, with a little bub on the way and a beautiful home.

It doesn't happen for everyone. But it happens. Timing, patience and luck.

— Camille in Vic

Manners maketh the man

The worst date I ended up on was with a guy off Hinge.

I showed up to the date to find him already on a date with another girl.

Too afraid to approach, I asked the waitstaff if they could confirm who the booking was under at that table. They confirmed it was him.

After about 30 seconds of feeling awkward, I decided to make my way to their table. Turns out, the two were just working out that they were both on the wrong date and it was a case of mistaken identity.

I was happy to laugh it off. It could have even been a funny story to tell our kids someday if we worked out … that was until we sat down.

He told me how relieved he was that the other girl wasn't his date because she wasn't "hot enough" and was "too old and ugly".

The date was pretty much over for me from there.

— Jude in Vic

Hijacking cupid's seat

I'm a woman in her 30s who, two years ago, decided to take things into her own hands. I was sick of waiting for men to come to me, and even more sick of dating apps going nowhere.

Over the past couple of years, if I find someone charming, I will ask them out.

I've learnt it's a muscle you can train; it only gets easier the more you do it.

This new approach has resulted in some of the most incredible connections with people who are mostly all still in my life.

I've met them at parties and gigs, in shops where they work, in a language class, at bars and even a kebab shop.

It's a powerful feeling when you realise your life is in your own hands.

If you want something, tap it on the shoulder…

— Lucy, Vic

The life-changing trip

We met on Bumble.

Neither of us expected anything that serious.

But his visa was about to expire and we didn't want to stop hanging out.

After several serious conversations and an overseas trip to meet his family, we applied for a partner visa a few months after we met.

Eight years, one dog, one wedding and one baby later — my life is better than I ever thought possible!

— Brydie in Boronia, Vic

Is it time to get off the carousel?

I found a long-term girlfriend on Hinge … when I lived in New York. But app dating in Sydney has been an absolute dumpster fire.

The effort is minimal, with so many users copying the exact same tired prompt responses … if they bother sharing about themselves at all. If you're lucky enough to get a match, they often don't reply, and the few who do agree to dates seem to be hunting for unicorns rather than actually getting to know someone.

To be fair, why should they invest when the apps create an illusion of infinite choice?

What strikes me most is, I've seen several women still on Hinge from years ago from when I last lived in Sydney.

It seems we're all so busy swiping that we're missing what's right in front of us.

— Tony in Wollstonecraft, NSW

Walking a tight rope

As a 55-year-old single woman, modern dating is akin to a delicately balanced scale teetering between hopefulness and hopelessness.

Maybe it's the Canberra bubble — a small "pool" — but it's hard to stop your mind running away with creeping thoughts that you are no longer youthful, no longer desirable. Invisible.

I've come to realise I am a singular woman whose depth, warmth and kindness don't jump out on an app — though perhaps that's true for many of us. My skin might be sagging a little, my wrinkles deeper. But my smile still shines, my laugh strong, my wit sharp.

As time passes, I accept that maybe I won't find my person — at least not on the apps. But I pursue the joys that fill me up. Maybe I will meet him IRL!

So the balance continues its teetering…

Today, it's hope.

— Nicole in Calwell, ACT

Trust your instincts

My partner and I met on Bumble.

I'd been on apps for years and had plenty of dates (both good and bad).

They'd just agreed to make a profile so a friend would as well.

We hit it off pretty quickly over messages and on our first date, we both got this feeling that the other one was going to be a significant person in our lives somehow.

We've been together for three years now, live together, and have a dog.

— Weyturner in SA

Raising the white flag

Dating sites have become a nightmare.

Most profiles are bots from overseas and it's rare to find a real person that actually wants to chat and meet for a date.

People are very cautious and cagey about direct contact or meeting, which is the whole point of a dating site.

It's become a complete waste of time.

I've given up … and will need to go back to actually meeting real people at events or trying speed dating events.

— John in Sydney

One coincidence, too many!

I had been separated for 10 years and put up a profile on an app for mature people at the age 60.

I saw a profile and thought he sounded great but I had decided I was never going to be the one to reach out.

Two weeks later, he messaged me the day after my divorce from my first husband had been finalised!

It turned out we had been in similar circles and had almost met repeatedly over about 20 years.

I even tried to purchase a property that he used to live in.

I finally met him 10 years later and we have been blissfully together for over six years.

— Susan in Woodend, Vic

Redefining relationship goals

I met June on a dating app some years ago, and we met for coffee.

Both in our late 50s, we found we had mutual friends from where we grew up.

Unexpectedly, we fell deeply in love. Although that's perhaps what everyone on these apps hopes for.

Later I asked her to marry. At the same time, I gave up a chance at a good career move so we could live together. We didn't.

After that things went sour. Maybe we had different expectations. Fourteen years later, we have our own lives and live in different places.

However, we still meet a few times a year and often have long phone conversations. We sometimes travel together.

You might say we persist at being very good friends.

That's a relationship goal worth aiming for.

— Jay in Canberra, ACT

Hate the game, not the player

Modern dating is difficult.

Over the last few years, I've been improving myself consistently.

I'm under 30. I work out often. I'm healthy. I love to read and cook. I own an apartment by the beach. I keep my apartment nice and tidy. And I have a loving family and great friends.

My attitude to dating is showing the same attention to someone as I do in other aspects of my life and that means being dutiful. I also feel that how you act and behave generally says much more about a person than mere words can.

Ultimately, all of this is not enough because I feel dating apps limit how you can present yourself by not showing people's nuances, which really show someone's character.

— Lucas in St Kilda, Melbourne

A window of opportunity

After losing my wife to cancer, I tried online dating for the first time at 67.

After one unsuccessful hook-up with a lady in another state, I let the membership lapse.

Two months later, the dating site offered me a three-day free trial and after some hesitation I tried again.

That's when I met my current wife, who was also on the same three-day trial and she lived in my city.

Chats turned to phone calls, then meeting up for coffee.

Two years married now and very happy.

— George in Kingsley, WA

The perfect offline and online pairing

As an older person, I couldn't get my mind around having to impress someone with my witty texts before I got to actually talk with them! So, oddly, my let's meet for a coffee strategic opening line was a failure!

But, there are one or more groups out there organising triple blind dates.

Three men and three women, age appropriate, at a decent restaurant, nice food and typically good conversation. A pleasant night out, even if you don't find friendship.

After a few, I found love and we have recently celebrated our first year together.

So yes, dating IRL is still a thing!

We subsequently found that we were both registered on the same dating app and rated as a brilliant match. Who knew? Not us!

— Robert, NSW

Game, set, match!

Not gonna lie, internet dating can feel like a cage-fight.

Would-be lovers often left feeling dazed, dizzy and wounded.

Stay strong, my mystery lover. The Venga Boys assure us happiness is just around the corner!

— Rodney in Wangaratta, Vic

Want to share your modern dating story?

We're on the hunt for short stories that shed light on love in 2026.

Whether you've shed tears of joy, sadness or even laughter in the process, we want to hear it all. (Promise, we won't judge!)

Your submissions will help expand our understanding of this topic and maybe make someone out there feel less alone, or warm and fuzzy on the inside.

Share your modern-dating story with us here.

World.title: The Pacific is full of diversity but some people want to make themselves whiter
World.content:
Pauline Bourke remembers when skin brighteners became popular in the early 2000s.

She now sells beauty products to Tongan youth who are continuing the trend.

"I believe they use these products to become more beautiful, their skin becomes more clearer … [they hope] their girlfriend or their boyfriend will also see them as more beautiful," she told ABC's The Pacific.

Skin whiteners and brighteners are common in Tonga.

Whiteness is a beauty ideal some Pacific people strive for, while those with darker skin tones are often discriminated against.

It is defined as colourism — the prejudicial or preferential treatment of people, usually of the same race, based on their skin tone.

Pauline Bourke says young people in Tonga continue to buy skin-whitening products. (ABC News: Marian Kupu)

The issue of whiteness can be traced back to the region's colonial past, and today some are fighting back against it.

'My offence is that I'm Black'

As Apple TV's Chief of War cast accepted the best ensemble performance award at the Film Independent Spirit Awards, Black-Hawaiian actor Moses Goods spoke in Native Hawaiian.

The celebration was short-lived when he was targeted by online trolls.

"I know we should let these things go and pay them no mind, and usually I do, but this one was different," Goods said on Instagram.

"This one was rooted in hatred and racism and not only that, it was from another Native Hawaiian.

"I'm a f****** popolo [Black person] with no koko — no Hawaiian blood, using the N-word freely and laughing about it.

"It'd be one thing if I did something offensive, but what was my offence? My offence is that I'm Black."

Moses Goods has spoken out against the hate he received online. (Supplied: Apple TV)

The issue does not only exist online, with 531pi radio host Carolanne Toetu'u noting it had permeated parts of Pacific culture.

"Growing up into a teenager, you'd say things like, 'what a waste, they're so good-looking but they are Black,'" Ms Toetu'u said.

Pacific's past linked to colourism

Maile Arvin, an expert in race and settler colonialism at the University of Hawaii, told the ABC that these attitudes were influenced by the Pacific's history.

"It's most obvious in the name Melanesia which refers to the Black islands," Dr Arvin said.

"Polynesia, the word just means many islands. And then Micronesia means small islands. So, the actual names are not racial in the sense that Melanesia is."

She said 19th and 20th century anthropologists like Louis Sullivan portrayed Polynesians as "whiter and nobler".

Sullivan took physical measurements and photographs, compiling data such as hair types and nose lengths to justify his claims.

Despite the work being debunked, Dr Arvin believed this history of elevating whiteness continued to influence Pacific societies.

"There is sometimes some understanding that Melanesians are understood to be folks with the darker skin, and therefore have a particular history with really explicit racism against them, which is tied to that," she said.

"I think it's important to see it as an origin story of the way we often unconsciously believe certain racial ideals in contemporary life."

May Hasola was left hurt and disappointed by the abuse she received. (Supplied: Solomon Islands Government)

Melanesian contestants competing at beauty pageants have also experienced colourism in recent years.

May Torowi Hasola represented Papua New Guinea at the regional competition in 2024 where she received a torrent of abuse for her skin tone.

How an ugly colonial legacy has roiled Pacific Island beauty pageants Beauty pageants remain serious business in the Pacific, but contestants are thinking twice before entering due to online bullying and discrimination.

"It was disappointing experiencing colourism, and especially when I put myself out to be of service, and to be someone who really champions women here in Papua New Guinea," Ms Hasola said.

"I was really blessed that I had such a strong family and people and friends that I could … rely on to uplift me and hold me during this time."

Despite the online abuse, she said the role was one of "the biggest honours of my life" and that she represented all regions in PNG.

Diversity is something Moses Goods wants people to celebrate.

He said events like FestPAC, the Pacific's largest arts and culture festival, were critical for learning from other cultures and celebrating difference.

"When you're in the middle of that environment and you see the different beautiful shades around you and know that we're all connected, we all come from the same thing," he said.

You can watch the full story and episode of The Pacific on iView.

World.title: Leaked data shows NT diphtheria cases surged a month before alert was issued
World.content:
Leaked NT Health data reveals diphtheria numbers surged in the Northern Territory a month before a public health alert was issued.

The data circulated by the department on Thursday to service providers has offered the first public insight into when diphtheria cases started growing in the NT, and the regions that were hit the hardest.

According to the document, a handful of diphtheria cases were recorded in the NT in early January, before multiple cases began to be recorded week on week across Darwin, the Top End and the Katherine region from the last week of February onwards.

NT Health did not issue a public health alert pertaining to the outbreak of diphtheria until March 25.

On Thursday last week, Federal Health Minister Mark Butler said the Northern Territory government requested assistance from the Commonwealth in late-April.

The current outbreak of diphtheria has been Australia's worst since records began in 1991.

Mark Butler says the federal government did not receive a request for support from the NT government until late-April. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

NT Health tight-lipped on outbreak data

The ABC has previously requested a breakdown of diphtheria cases by region from NT Health but did not receive a response.

The NT stands in stark contrast to health departments in Western Australia and Queensland which provide public online data about case numbers and locations.

Earlier this week Paul Burgess said diphtheria cases were spread across the NT, but did not offer any specifics. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

At a press conference on Tuesday, NT Chief Health Officer Dr Paul Burgess said the outbreak had spread all throughout the NT but did not provide specifics.

"It's actually all over the five regions of the Northern Territory," he said.

NT diphtheria cases declining as 10,000 immunised, one death confirmed The NT government says the rate of new diphtheria cases in the territory has fallen from more than 20 per week to less than 10 after 10,000 Territorians stepped up to be immunised against the ongoing outbreak.

An NT Health spokesperson has confirmed the legitimacy of the data leaked to the ABC but said it was not intended to be shared with the public.

"The daily epi curve chart is part of a diphtheria clinical briefing intended for clinicians and service providers and is not produced for public distribution," the statement read.

"Changes may occur even daily as information comes to light for places of acquisition."

While it is correct the number of cases recorded for any given day did often change in subsequent reporting, two daily charts seen by the ABC showed the data was always altered to a higher figure.

This means the data provided in some daily reports were a conservative estimate of the real case numbers.

NT Health has confirmed one diphtheria death in the NT since the outbreak began.

Vaccines rolled out in force as case numbers rise

The data shows aggregate case numbers have decreased in the last three weeks, in accordance with statements made by the NT Health Minister and Chief Health Officer.

"We have seen a reduction in the number of reported cases, and whilst we're not out of the woods it is important to recognise that reduction has continued," Health Minister Steve Edgington said on Tuesday.

Earlier this week Steve Edgington said diphtheria case numbers had continued to drop. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

It comes amid a wide-scale vaccine roll-out by the Territory and Federal governments.

On Tuesday last week, the Commonwealth announced a $7.2 million funding package for mitigating the spread of diphtheria.

Cases of the disease have simultaneously been spreading across Australia.

On Friday, the Australian Centre for Disease Control (CDC) reported more than 260 cases in Australia in 2026, with 159 cases in the Northern Territory, 102 in Western Australia, 6 in South Australia and less than five in Queensland.

More than 10,000 people have been vaccinated against diphtheria over the past few months. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Figures from the respective states' health departments have differed slightly from the CDC's, with state health teams reporting 98 cases for Western Australia, seven in South Australia, and three cases in Queensland as of Friday.

On Tuesday, NT Health Minister Steve Edgington indicated on Tuesday 163 cases had been identified in the NT, of which 115 were cutaneous and 48 were respiratory.

World.title: Hopes pinned on promising sequel to prevent a Whyalla wipeout
World.content:
"We've seen this movie before" is a phrase that sums up the way many people feel about the Whyalla steelworks' financial predicament.

For decades, the plant has endured multiple ownership changes and, more recently, has struggled to even produce steel.

But the community is hopeful a promising new sequel is on the way for the lifeblood of the town.

"The last administration was run by the banks," Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union organiser Steve McMillan said.

"This time it's the state and federal governments that have got buy-in."

Mr McMillan represents some of the workers at the Whyalla steelworks, many of whom are going through their second administration in a decade.

Steve McMillan says the community and steelworkers are aware of the likelihood of job losses. (ABC News)

In 2016, former steelworks owner Arrium folded.

Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance took over, before that business also failed and was forced into administration by the South Australian government in February last year.

Nearly 16 months later, another attempt to deliver a sustainable future for the Whyalla steelworks, and the city of 22,000 people that relies on it, is taking shape.

What's in play?

On Wednesday, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas and administrator Korda Mentha unveiled the final two bidders left in the process to take over the steelworks and its associated mines and port.

Australian-owned company M Resources and Indian steelmaker Jindal Steel are in the running and hope to secure the $1.9 billion on offer from the federal and state governments.

Australia's biggest steelmaker, BlueScope Steel, also retains the right to make a final offer.

Making his pitch for the steelworks, M Resources founder and president Matt Latimore said it was important to secure sovereign steelmaking in Australian hands.

Matt Latimore's M Resources is one of two final bidders for the Whyalla steelworks. (Supplied)

"Sovereign steelmaking would be for important industries in Australia like the rail construction and defence, which Whyalla currently supplies," he told ABC News.

"We believe we're well qualified with a plan to execute the transformation of the Whyalla steelworks from the current blast furnace aging operation to a new relatively small to medium-sized electric arc furnace."

The blast furnace at the heart of the Whyalla steelworks was built in the 1960s and has not been substantially upgraded since 2004.

It has been shut down since early April.

The aging blast furnace inside the Whyalla steelworks has been offline since early April. (Supplied)

Marty Hilton worked at the blast furnace for 45 years and retired last year.

He said it created iron that was then turned into steel in another part of the plant.

"It's the iron that everything else relies on," the former worker said.

"Getting it going again [is] a tricky thing.

"A furnace can get cold quite quickly, but we can also get it running again quite quickly too if all the ducks line up."

Marty Hilton worked for more than four decades at the Whyalla plant. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Mr Malinauskas said the ongoing blast furnace shutdown highlighted the urgent need for the steelworks to be modernised.

"There's a critical six to eight weeks ahead for the blast furnace to try and bring it back up to life," he said.

"None of that really dissuades anyone from the optimistic future that this town has if we get this plan right."

'No steelworks, no town': Whyalla's fight for a future While the steelmaking city of Whyalla is no stranger to struggle, the latest crisis is taking a severe toll on the population, who very much want to continue making steel for Australia but say they are "sick of having to be resilient".

That plan is to continue to use part of the existing steelmaking process, while replacing the blast furnace with a direct reduction iron (DRI) facility and an electric arc furnace (EAF).

But to order, build and install that infrastructure is expected to cost several hundreds of millions of dollars and take two to three years.

The blast furnace is not expected to last that long, even if it can be brought back online.

"Now if it comes to pass that there is a requirement for redundancies or whatever that looks like, you can rest assured that we'll comply with our enterprise agreements, we'll work with the unions, we'll work with the state to manage that as best we can," KordaMentha partner Sebastian Hams said on Wednesday.

Questions over jobs

Mr Latimore said he was aware of the blast furnace issue and potential workforce implications.

"Those numbers are still to be totally refined in terms of how many workers will be required for the transition and what workers will take what roles in that optimised process," he said.

But the M Resources boss said a mine expansion could deliver some extra jobs.

Some Whyalla locals are uncertain about what the future holds. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr McMillan said steel workers were aware that there was the potential for job losses.

"Everything that humanly possible could be done is being done," he said.

"If it falls over, it falls over.

"There's going to be an impact and everyone that works out there and in the community quite clearly know that."

Loading...

But local contractor Chris Fewster said he felt KordaMentha had not kept the community adequately informed.

"I don't have faith anymore in really any of the governments because I don't have the information that I can believe in myself to make that decision," he said.

"Where's the information that I can hang my hat on that something good is going to come out of this?

"I see a lot of money going out to KordaMentha, public money, and I don't see a result that I can really get my head around.

"So unless something happens that's nothing like what happened before, then I'm pretty fearful."

Timeline of GFG's crisis-plagued steelworks Whyalla's steelworks has gone into administration for the second time in under a decade. Here is a look at how events have unfolded in the city in recent years.

Taxpayers have so far spent more than $700 million on the administration process, including about $3 million each month for KordaMentha.

With the sale process not expected to conclude until the end of the year, that total cost could increase with additional money expected to be allocated in South Australia's state budget handed down on Thursday.

But with the federal and state governments putting an increased focus on local manufacturing in recent years, there is hope the Whyalla story could finally have a happy ending.

"I think you know in five years' time it actually could be the first ever good news story … if you've got the right company that comes in and takes over," Mr Hilton said.

Whyalla Mayor Phill Stone agreed, crediting the state government intervention as the turning point for the town.

Phill Stone says governments are aware of the importance of the Whyalla steelworks. (ABC News: James Wakelin)

"That will go down in history, in my view, as the saving of Whyalla," he said.

"This time we've got governments … aware of the importance of steelmaking within Australia, aware of how Whyalla must be saved, not just for Whyalla, not just for the 22,000-odd that live here, it's for the benefit of the whole nation."

World.title: The simple, ordinary joy of Kylie Minogue
World.content:
Is the struggle to understand Kylie finally over?

Has the three-part Netflix documentary, Kylie, answered the question that has nagged at bewildered commentators, critics, music writers, cool magazine editors and the rest of the legacy media for so long?

Like amateur alchemists trying to separate gold into its constituent parts, those critics and the media have wrung their hands to the bone trying to figure out the unparalleled success of someone to whom the rest of us have been simply, joyously dancing for decades.

How, they anguish, can someone be such a cultural phenomenon, so successful, so broadly adored when they are so… ordinary?

Kylie Minogue reveals 'secret' cancer and IVF struggles in Netflix doco "Our Kylie" gets candid in the three-part Netflix docuseries, grieving over IVF struggles, Michael Hutchence, and revealing she was diagnosed with cancer a second time in 2021.

The ordinariness of Kylie Minogue is both her mystery and her superpower. We are easier with our pop gods being strange. The contemptuousness of Madonna; the otherworldliness of David Bowie; the absolute freakery of Michael Jackson.

But present to the world like a cheerful, well-balanced Rick Astley, and the music world will roll its eyes at you, even while your banging pop songs bring every single person in the room onto the dancefloor.

It's the music that turns out to be undeniable, as the music always is when it's that good. That reality persists through time and space and brings us to the apex of the brilliant career of Kylie Minogue and her now absolute undeniability.

She is the only female music artist in UK history to have number-one albums in five consecutive decades. A fan base that encompasses the entire globe. Grammy awards, and the largest Glastonbury crowd of all time. More than 80 million records sold worldwide.

All this, from a performer with the lifestyle and demeanour of that really nice girl you went to high school with.

This series is unflinching

The contrasts are wonderful. As Michael Harte's Netflix documentary hits the number-one position around the world this week, Kylie Minogue celebrated her 58th birthday. She posted her dinner with friends, and her small, generic chocolate birthday cake that looked straight out of Coles. It had one candle, and all her besties singing to her, slightly out of key.

It's impossible not to compare that simple, happy evening with how you imagine that other, wannabe Kylie — Jenner — would have celebrated her birthday… surely there would have at least been some elephants?

Kylie Minogue in the music video for her 2000 single Spinning Around. (Supplied: Paulo Sutch)

The series is unflinching about the years of abuse heaped on Kylie from those bewildered at her success. I was a reporter at The Age during her transition from the bubble-gum of the Stock Aitken Waterman years into something more serious, and I flinch now as I recall the casual misogyny, cruelty and contempt with which she was routinely dismissed in the newsroom of the city from which she came.

You'd think there'd be some Melbourne pride in there as Kylie left Neighbours and conquered the UK and many European markets with her perfect pop. But no. Instead, it was the Sunday edition of my paper, and the reporter, Anthony Dennis, now a travel writer, who coined the brutal, highly adhesive moniker, The Singing Budgie.

There will be reporters today, like this one, who I hope will be cringing in shame at how they treated her.

The secret of her enormous appeal

The documentary has an unusual awkwardness to it. The interviews mostly appear to be just the chance result of leaving a camera on and waiting for Kylie to find her thoughts or decide to reveal something.

And the deciding itself is often the most compelling element: you can clearly see the decision-making process, the choice that a deeply private albeit hugely successful star is making to reveal herself. That unaffected candour, again, so surprising in contrast to more carefully constructed artists.

And wrapped around and through Kylie's life story is that affecting and deeply connecting cheerfulness and resilience that seems to confound her critics most of all. It's clear from miles of footage over five decades that Kylie's self-belief has remained rock solid from her earliest London days: her work ethic was impressive, her choices were always deliberate, never panicky — duets with Robbie Williams and Nick Cave come to mind — and she had the Kevlar protection of her family to keep her undistracted from her ambitions. You can see it now as the fearsome combination that it has always been.



So, what is revealed as the secret to Kylie's enormous appeal? The documentary hands that question to the Prince of Darkness himself, Nick Cave, who explains it with more laughter and crinkling smiles than I have ever seen from this man — and I've watched almost every interview he's ever done.

Wreathed in delight, Nick explains that like pop music itself, Kylie is a joy machine, a positive, life-affirming source of joy and rapture. His exhortation to her to get back on the dance floor with her pop songs sparked one of her most creative, and successful periods, including the immortal, hot-panted Spinning Around.

But in the end, a woman who has had her wins and her losses, her terrors and her triumphs, and who regularly goes back to stay with her family in suburban Melbourne, has become one of the music legends of her time, and it's not that hard to figure out why.

It's simple, ordinary. Joy. Just joy.

This weekend we have birds, dogs and mushrooms, and if you haven't yet seen the Kylie doco, you've got that to look forward to, as well.

Have a safe and happy weekend and pity my dilemma in having to select just one Kylie song for you. This ecstatic moment from Kylie's Tension tour last year was probably my live music highlight and, as Nick says, is everything we love about live, fabulous dance music. Crank this one — it'll lift you higher.

Well done, Kylie — keep going well.

Virginia Trioli is presenter of Creative Types and a former co-host of ABC News Breakfast and Mornings on ABC Radio Melbourne.

World.title: How much it costs to live in Sydney’s most expensive suburb
World.content:
PropertyNewsNSW residential property How much it costs to live in Sydney’s most expensive suburb Sue Williams May 30, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Buy an average kind of house on a middling piece of land in what’s become Australia’s priciest suburb – and you’ll have no change left from a staggering $11 million. And what’s more, you might just have bought yourself the most expensive knockdown-rebuild you could ever imagine. The median house price in the Sydney eastern suburbs’ enclave of Bellevue Hill has hit an all-time high. The median house price in the Sydney eastern suburbs’ enclave of Bellevue Hill has hit an all-time high at $11 million, after skyrocketing by 29.3 per cent in the 12 months to March, according to latest Domain figures. It’s a price growth that shows no sign, either, of tailing off like parts of the nation’s property market. By comparison, Sydney house prices jumped by 6.6 per cent over the year to March.



“It’s an incredible median house price for an Australian suburb,” said Domain’s chief of research and economics Dr Nicola Powell, of Bellevue Hill. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Seek co-founder to find new owner for $11 million Sydney residence “That’s a function of the scarcity of supply in the suburb, with only 83 sales in the last year which is a very limited turnover with houses there very tightly held. “So when the right house comes along, that can create a real jump in price as the ultra-wealthy, who are less affected by cash rate hikes and the rising cost of living, are happy to pay whatever it takes to buy a rare trophy asset. With deeply embedded wealth, they see buying expensive houses as a means of long-term wealth preservation.” While Bellevue Hill has no direct harbour, river or beach frontage, it’s still Australia’s most expensive suburb, according to the latest Domain House Price Report, with regular top-end sales in the many tens of millions.



In the past year alone, it’s seen sales for $50 million at 69 Victoria Road, $26 million at 106 Victoria Road, $24.5 million at 33 Streatfield Road and $21,550, 000 at 6 Latimer Road. Last year also saw Gretel Packer pay $59 million for a property next door to her Bellevue Hill home. Gretel Packer added to her Bellevue Hill compound in 2025. With the 2026 federal budget reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax, that price growth looks set only to continue, Powell believes. “Over time, we’re going to see people pumping more and more wealth into their primary home because they won’t need to pay tax on it,” she said. “They’ll favour massive renovations or extensions over buying other investment property, which will push prices up even higher.”





But it’s not as if that median of $11 million will buy you the house of your dreams, either. Sales agent Oliver Lavers of TRG says it’s much more likely it’ll leave you with a house that’ll need a fair bit of work to bring it up to scratch. “In February this year I sold a four-bedroom house at 18 Bunyula Road for $10.4 million which is being knocked down and rebuilt as a dual occupancy duplex,” said Lavers, who’s also now selling 34 Beresford Road for that magic median $11 million – although it’s right on the cusp of Rose Bay and Bellevue Hill. This Bunyula Road property is set to be knocked down. “But Bellevue Hill is so popular not only because of the calibre of some of its properties, but also they’re big homes on good sizes of land. Then it’s also very convenient with prestige schools nearby, and being close to the city and Bondi Junction, and all the facilities.”



Ironically, however, while the median house price in Bellevue Hill is surging, the median apartment price is falling, down 8.1 per cent over the last 12 months to March a median of $1,655,000. “The profile of unit buyers in Bellevue Hill is very different to the house buyers,” said Powell. “They’re still paying for the prestige location, but interest rate and cost of living rises are hitting them harder and there’s not the scarcity of apartments that there is for the prestige houses.”
